writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XLVI,” how does Austen show scandal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XLVI, how does Austen develop the idea of scandal? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLVI develops the idea of scandal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XLVI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of scandal. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XLVI suggests about scandal. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's plot and conflict), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XLVI to complicate the reader's understanding of scandal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of scandal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XLVI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of scandal follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XLVI and its treatment of scandal. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's plot and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XLVI as evidence for a larger claim about scandal in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of scandal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the chapter for structure, characterization (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about scandal? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Chapter XLVI develops the idea of scandal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Lydia's elopement shows how a single act can destroy a whole family's reputation. When the text says “Though Lydia’s short letter to Mrs. F. gave them to understand that they were going to Gretna Green, something was dropped by Denny expressing his belief that W. never intended to go there” (Chapter XLVI, paragraph 5), it shows this directly. Jane's letter fears that Wickham "never intended" to go to Gretna Green, where they could marry, and Elizabeth at once assumes Darcy will withdraw, because Lydia's disgrace attaches to every sister.

followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Lydia's elopement shows how a single act can destroy a whole family's reputation. Useful evidence: “thanked him with tears of gratitude” (Chapter XLVI, paragraph 26): Elizabeth's response to her uncle's promise of help: the family closes ranks. On characterization: Elizabeth tells Darcy everything in her distress, and he leaves abruptly; she assumes, wrongly, that the scandal has ended his regard. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Lydia, 16, runs off with Wickham, an adult. Frame it as exploitation of a minor and discuss the period's double standard that blames her.
contentNotes.studentPreview: A 16-year-old runs away with an adult man. We will discuss who holds power here.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Who is blamed for the elopement, and is that fair?”
